question: What is method-level security in Spring Security?
title: Method-Level Security in Spring Security — @PreAuthorize
direct_answer: **Method-level security** applies access control directly on service methods using annotations like `@PreAuthorize`, `@PostAuthorize`, and `@Secured`. Enabled with `@EnableMethodSecurity` on your configuration class. Provides fine-grained security beyond URL-based rules.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of fine-grained security beyond URL patterns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @EnableMethodSecurity is required to activate method security
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show @PreAuthorize with SpEL expressions accessing method parameters

sections.title: Method Security Annotations
Method Security Annotations
sections.content:
- **`@EnableMethodSecurity`**: Required to activate method-level security (Spring 6)
- **`@PreAuthorize`**: Evaluated BEFORE method executes — if fails, method not called, `AccessDeniedException` thrown
- **`@PostAuthorize`**: Evaluated AFTER method executes — can access `returnObject`
- **`@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")`**: Simpler — just role-based, no SpEL
- **SpEL expressions**: `hasRole('ADMIN')`, `hasAnyRole('ADMIN','MANAGER')`, `isAuthenticated()`, `#param == authentication.name`
- **`#paramName`**: Access method parameter by name in SpEL
- **`authentication`**: Current `Authentication` object in SpEL
- **`returnObject`**: Method return value in `@PostAuthorize`
- **Applied to**: Any Spring bean method — service, repository, controller

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Method-level security lets you put access control directly on service methods using annotations. You enable it with @EnableMethodSecurity on your configuration class. Then you can annotate service methods with @PreAuthorize and Spring Security checks the condition before the method runs. If the check fails, it throws AccessDeniedException and the method never executes. The power is in SpEL expressions — you can write hasRole('ADMIN'), check multiple roles with hasAnyRole, or even compare method parameters to the current user. For example, @PreAuthorize('#userId == authentication.principal.id') lets users access only their own data. @PostAuthorize is less common but useful when you need to verify the returned data belongs to the current user.

seo.metaTitle: Method-Level Security in Spring Security | Java Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn method-level security in Spring Security — @EnableMethodSecurity, @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @Secured, SpEL expressions, parameter access.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: URL-based security tells you who can access which endpoint — method-level security tells you who can access which data. Both are needed, and most codebases only implement the first.

beats.content: Method-level security lets you put access control annotations directly on service methods. You enable it by adding @EnableMethodSecurity to your configuration class — without that annotation, the annotations are silently ignored.

@PreAuthorize is the main annotation. You give it a SpEL expression, and Spring Security evaluates it before the method runs. If the expression returns false, it throws AccessDeniedException immediately — the method never executes.

The real power comes from SpEL. You can do more than role checks: @PreAuthorize('#userId == authentication.principal.id') lets a user access only their own data. @PreAuthorize('hasRole(ADMIN) or #userId == authentication.principal.id') adds an admin override. URL security can't express either of those patterns.
candidates miss: in Spring Security 6, the annotation is @EnableMethodSecurity, not the older @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity. If you use the old one in a Spring Boot 3 app it won't work.

speakable_v2.cap: Enable with @EnableMethodSecurity, annotate service methods with @PreAuthorize, write SpEL. Three steps for data-level security that URL rules can't provide.
followup_handoff: @PostAuthorize is the companion annotation — it checks authorization after the method runs, with access to the return value.
The difference between @PreAuthorize and the older @Secured is worth knowing — especially since @Secured needs extra setup in Spring 6.

question: What is the difference between @PreAuthorize and @Secured?
title: @PreAuthorize vs @Secured in Spring Security
direct_answer: **`@PreAuthorize`** uses **SpEL expressions** — powerful, flexible: `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') and #age > 18")`. **`@Secured`** uses simple role name strings — limited to role checks only: `@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")`. Always prefer `@PreAuthorize` for its flexibility.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to choose the right annotation for the use case
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Secured when @PreAuthorize's flexibility would help — or forgetting @Secured needs ROLE_ prefix
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a real-world @PreAuthorize example with parameter access that @Secured couldn't do

sections.title: @PreAuthorize vs @Secured
Comparison Table
sections.content:
| Aspect | @PreAuthorize | @Secured |
|--------|---------------|----------|
| Language | SpEL | String array |
| Expressiveness | High | Low (roles only) |
| Method params | ✓ (`#param`) | ✗ |
| Return object | via @PostAuthorize | ✗ |
| ROLE_ prefix | Not needed (hasRole adds it) | Required |
| Recommendation | ✓ Preferred | Legacy, simple cases |

- **Enable `@Secured`**: Needs `@EnableMethodSecurity(securedEnabled=true)` (disabled by default in Spring 6)
- **`@PreAuthorize` enabled**: By default with `@EnableMethodSecurity`
- **`@RolesAllowed`**: JSR-250 annotation — equivalent to @Secured, needs `jsr250Enabled=true`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @PreAuthorize and @Secured both protect method execution, but they differ in power. @Secured is simple — you give it role name strings, and it checks if the current user has any of those roles. The downsides: you must include the ROLE_ prefix yourself, and you can only do role checks — no SpEL, no method parameter access. @PreAuthorize takes a SpEL expression, which gives you a lot more power: you can check roles without the prefix using hasRole, combine conditions with AND/OR, access method parameters with #paramName, and check if the user is accessing their own data. For any non-trivial authorization check, @PreAuthorize is the right choice. @Secured is mainly seen in older codebases or when simplicity is preferred for basic role checks.

seo.metaDescription: Compare @PreAuthorize and @Secured in Spring Security — SpEL vs role strings, method parameter access, ROLE_ prefix, when to use each.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: @Secured and @PreAuthorize both protect methods, but one is essentially a subset of the other — and in Spring Security 6, they're not even both on by default.

beats.content: @Secured is the older, simpler annotation. You give it a role name string and it checks if the user has that role. That's all it can do. You must include the ROLE_ prefix yourself, and you can't write complex conditions or reference method parameters.

@PreAuthorize takes a SpEL expression, which gives you full flexibility. Role checks without the prefix via hasRole, combining conditions with AND and OR, accessing method arguments with #paramName, comparing to the current user's identity — all possible.

non-obvious: in Spring Security 6, @EnableMethodSecurity enables @PreAuthorize by default but @Secured is disabled. To use @Secured you must pass securedEnabled=true to the annotation. This surprises people who migrate from Spring Boot 2.

speakable_v2.cap: @PreAuthorize is the right choice for almost every case. @Secured exists in legacy codebases — know its ROLE_ prefix requirement and that it needs explicit activation in Spring 6.
followup_handoff: @RolesAllowed is a third option from JSR-250 — it's equivalent to @Secured but from the standard Java security annotations.
We can also look at the SpEL functions available in @PreAuthorize in more detail.

question: What SpEL expressions can you use in @PreAuthorize?
title: SpEL in @PreAuthorize — hasRole, hasAuthority, isAuthenticated, Principal Access
direct_answer: Common SpEL expressions in `@PreAuthorize`: `hasRole('ROLE')`, `hasAnyRole(...)`, `hasAuthority('PERM')`, `isAuthenticated()`, `isAnonymous()`, `#param == authentication.name` (param equality), `authentication.principal.id == #userId` (object field access).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing you can access method parameters with # prefix and authentication.principal properties
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the #userId == authentication.principal.id pattern for owner-only access

sections.title: SpEL Expression Examples
SpEL Reference
sections.content:
- **`hasRole('X')`**: Checks for authority `ROLE_X` — auto-prepends `ROLE_`
- **`hasAnyRole('X','Y')`**: User has X or Y role
- **`hasAuthority('X')`**: Exact authority string match — no prefix added
- **`isAuthenticated()`**: User is logged in (not anonymous)
- **`isAnonymous()`**: User is NOT logged in
- **`#paramName`**: Access method parameter by name (requires `-parameters` compiler flag or Spring's annotation introspection)
- **`authentication`**: Current `Authentication` object
- **`authentication.name`**: Username
- **`authentication.principal`**: UserDetails object
- **`authentication.principal.id`**: Field on your custom UserDetails implementation
- **`returnObject`**: Only in `@PostAuthorize` — the method's return value

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: SpEL in @PreAuthorize gives you powerful authorization expressions. The basics: hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix and checks the role, hasAuthority does an exact string match without prefix. isAuthenticated checks if the user is logged in. For data-level security — ensuring users can only access their own data — you use the #paramName syntax to reference method parameters and compare to the current user. So @PreAuthorize('#userId == authentication.principal.id') says 'this method can only be called if the userId parameter matches the current user's ID'. You access the current user via the authentication object — authentication.name for username, or authentication.principal for the full UserDetails object where you can access custom fields like id or email.

followup_questions: What is the difference between hasRole() and hasAuthority() in SpEL?
How do you access a custom field on your UserDetails in @PreAuthorize?

seo.metaDescription: Learn SpEL expressions in @PreAuthorize — hasRole, hasAuthority, isAuthenticated, #param access, authentication.principal, and owner-only access pattern.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: The #paramName syntax in @PreAuthorize is what makes data-level security possible — it's the difference between 'only admins' and 'only the owner or an admin'.

beats.content: The basic SpEL functions are hasRole, which checks for a role with the ROLE_ prefix added automatically, hasAuthority for an exact authority string match, and isAuthenticated to verify the user is logged in.

For data ownership checks, you use #paramName to reference a method parameter. @PreAuthorize('#userId == authentication.principal.id') means 'only allow this call if the userId argument matches the current user's ID'. You can combine with OR for an admin override: @PreAuthorize('hasRole(ADMIN) or #userId == authentication.principal.id').

The authentication object gives you access to the current user's full Authentication. authentication.name returns the username. authentication.principal returns your UserDetails object, where you can access custom fields like id or email if your UserDetails implementation has them.

gotcha: #paramName requires the method parameter names to be available at runtime. In Spring Boot this works by default via Spring's parameter name discovery. In some edge cases with interfaces, you may need the -parameters compiler flag or @Param annotations.

speakable_v2.cap: hasRole for roles, hasAuthority for exact permissions, #paramName for method argument access, authentication.principal for the current user's object. Combine with AND and OR for complex rules.
followup_handoff: @PostAuthorize has returnObject — a companion variable that gives you access to the method's return value after execution.
We can also look at @PreFilter and @PostFilter for filtering collection parameters and return values.

question: What is the difference between URL-based and method-level security?
title: URL-Based vs Method-Level Security in Spring — When to Use Each
direct_answer: **URL-based security** (`SecurityFilterChain`) coarsely protects endpoints by URL pattern and HTTP method. **Method-level security** (`@PreAuthorize`) provides fine-grained protection on specific service methods — can check object ownership, complex conditions, and applies even when service is called from non-HTTP contexts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Architecture thinking — when to use each layer of security
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using only URL security and missing data-level access control
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain defense in depth — use both layers together

sections.title: URL vs Method Security
Use Cases for Each
sections.content:
- **URL security**: Route-level access control — "only admins can access /admin/**"
- **Method security**: Data-level — "users can only access their own records"
- **Defense in depth**: Use BOTH — URL for coarse routing, methods for fine-grained data access
- **URL limitations**: Can't check object ownership, can't reference runtime data
- **Method security benefits**: Context-aware, can check method parameters and return values
- **Non-HTTP contexts**: Method security works when called from scheduled jobs, message consumers, etc.
- **Typical pattern**: URL rules = which endpoints exist for which roles; Method rules = who can access which data
- **Ordering**: URL security runs at filter level (before controller); Method security runs via AOP proxy (inside Spring context)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: URL-based and method-level security serve different granularities of protection. URL security is coarse — you say '/admin/** requires ADMIN role' and that's it. It's applied at the filter level before your code even runs. Method security is fine-grained — you can check not just roles but also whether the user owns the specific data being accessed. For example, you can't express 'a user can only read their own profile' with URL patterns alone, but you can with @PreAuthorize('#userId == authentication.principal.id'). Best practice is to use both layers together — defense in depth. URL security as the outer gate for routing, method security for data-level access control. Method security also works when your service is called from places other than HTTP — like scheduled tasks or message consumers.

seo.metaTitle: URL Security vs Method Security in Spring | Java Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn when to use URL-based vs method-level security in Spring — coarse-grained routing vs fine-grained data access, defense in depth, @PreAuthorize vs SecurityFilterChain.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: URL security and method security are at different layers — and using only one of them leaves a gap that's easy for interviewers to spot.

beats.content: URL-based security runs at the filter level before your code executes. It matches URL patterns and HTTP methods to role requirements — fast and effective for coarse routing. The limitation is that it can only see the URL, not what data is being accessed.

Method-level security runs inside the Spring application context via AOP proxies. It can check roles, but also object ownership, method parameters, and return values. It works whether the method is called from an HTTP request, a scheduled job, or a message listener.

The right approach uses both layers together. URL security as the outer gate: only users with the USER role can reach /api/users/**. Method security as the inner gate: a user can only read their own user record, not any other user's. URL rules can't express ownership — method rules can.

sharp edge: relying only on URL security is a common vulnerability. If a service method is called from a scheduled job or an internal service — not through an HTTP endpoint — URL security doesn't apply. Method security covers all call paths.

speakable_v2.cap: Use URL security for coarse-grained routing. Use method security for fine-grained data access. Defense in depth means both layers, not just one.
followup_handoff: Defense in depth as a security principle is worth elaborating on if the interviewer asks about general security approach.
We can also discuss where Spring Security's AOP proxy applies — only on Spring beans, not on direct method calls within the same class.

question: What is @PostAuthorize in Spring Security?
title: @PostAuthorize in Spring Security — Post-Method Authorization
direct_answer: **`@PostAuthorize`** evaluates a security expression AFTER the method executes and can access the method's **return value** via `returnObject`. Use it when authorization depends on the returned data itself — like ensuring the loaded document belongs to the current user.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @PostAuthorize exists and loading a record then checking ownership manually in service code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the performance implication — method runs before auth check, so DB hit happens before potential 403

sections.title: @PostAuthorize Usage
@PostAuthorize Details
sections.content:
- **`returnObject`**: SpEL variable holding the method's return value
- **Timing**: Method executes FIRST, then expression evaluated
- **On failure**: `AccessDeniedException` thrown AFTER method ran — the method's side effects already happened
- **Performance**: DB query runs even if user isn't authorized — consider @PreAuthorize if you can check ID beforehand
- **Use case**: When you need the returned data to make the authorization decision
- **`@PostFilter`**: Filters elements from a returned collection based on expression — `@PostFilter("filterObject.owner == authentication.name")`
- **`@PreFilter`**: Filters input collection before method executes
- **`@PostAuthorize` vs manual check**: Annotation is cleaner and handles null safety; Spring auto-throws 403

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @PostAuthorize is like @PreAuthorize but it runs after the method instead of before. It can access the return value through the returnObject variable in the SpEL expression. The classic use case is ownership verification when you need to load the object first to check who owns it — like loading a document and then verifying the owner field matches the current user. The performance consideration worth mentioning: because the method runs first, the database query happens regardless of the authorization outcome. If the check fails, Spring throws AccessDeniedException, but the method body already ran. This is generally acceptable for read operations, but you'd be more careful with write operations — prefer @PreAuthorize when you can validate before execution.

followup_questions: What are the performance implications of @PostAuthorize vs @PreAuthorize?
Can @PostAuthorize prevent side effects from already-executed methods?

seo.metaTitle: @PostAuthorize in Spring Security | Java Fresher Interview Guide
seo.metaDescription: Learn @PostAuthorize in Spring Security — post-method authorization, returnObject access, ownership verification, @PostFilter, and performance implications.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: @PostAuthorize solves an authorization problem @PreAuthorize can't — when you don't know if access is allowed until after you've fetched the data.

beats.content: @PostAuthorize evaluates its expression after the method runs. It exposes the return value through a returnObject variable in the SpEL expression. The classic case: loading a document and then checking that the owner field on the returned object matches the current user.

The difference from @PreAuthorize is timing. @PostAuthorize('returnObject.ownerUsername == authentication.name') on a getDocument method means: load the document, then check ownership. If the check fails, Spring throws AccessDeniedException — but the method already ran and the database query already happened.

production trap: because the method executes first, the DB hit always occurs regardless of whether the user is authorized. For read operations this is usually acceptable. For write operations — methods that modify data — you should prefer @PreAuthorize if you can check ownership by ID before execution. A @PostAuthorize on a delete method would delete the record and then fail authorization — the data is already gone.

speakable_v2.cap: @PostAuthorize is for when you need the returned object to make the authorization decision. Use @PreAuthorize whenever you can — it prevents execution entirely, including any side effects.
followup_handoff: @PostFilter filters collection return values — it removes elements from the returned list where the expression is false.
We can also look at the performance implications in detail and when a manual ownership check in service code is actually cleaner.

question: How do you test method-level security in Spring Boot?
title: Testing Method-Level Security — @WithMockUser and MockMvc
direct_answer: Use **`@WithMockUser`** to simulate an authenticated user in tests. For role-specific tests, `@WithMockUser(roles='ADMIN')`. Use **`MockMvc`** for controller tests. Verify that protected methods throw `AccessDeniedException` for unauthorized users.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not testing security — writing tests only for success scenarios
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both success (authorized) and failure (AccessDeniedException) test cases

sections.title: Testing Security with @WithMockUser
Security Testing Annotations
sections.content:
- **`@WithMockUser`**: Creates a mock authenticated user — default: username='user', password='password', roles=['USER']
- **`@WithMockUser(username='alice', roles='ADMIN')`**: Custom user
- **`@WithAnonymousUser`**: Unauthenticated user
- **`@WithUserDetails('alice')`**: Loads from your actual `UserDetailsService`
- **`MockMvc` + security**: Add `springSecurity()` to MockMvc for full security integration tests
- **`AccessDeniedException`**: Thrown when @PreAuthorize fails for authenticated user with wrong role
- **`AuthenticationCredentialsNotFoundException`**: Thrown when unauthenticated user accesses secured method
- **Test both paths**: Always test authorized (success) AND unauthorized (failure) scenarios
- **`spring-security-test` dependency**: `spring-boot-starter-test` includes this

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Testing method-level security in Spring Boot uses the @WithMockUser annotation from the spring-security-test module, which is included with spring-boot-starter-test. You annotate a test with @WithMockUser and specify the role — Spring Security sets up a mock authentication in the SecurityContext before the test runs. The test can then verify that the service method executes successfully for authorized users and throws AccessDeniedException for unauthorized ones. It's important to test both paths: the happy path with the correct role, and the failure case with insufficient permissions. You'd also use @WithAnonymousUser to test that completely unauthenticated access is rejected. For controller tests with MockMvc, you'd set up the MockMvc with springSecurity() to apply the full security filter chain.

seo.metaDescription: Learn to test method-level security in Spring Boot — @WithMockUser, @WithAnonymousUser, AccessDeniedException assertions, MockMvc security tests.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: Testing security means testing both the success path and the rejection path — most developers test that authorized users get in, but forget to test that unauthorized users get kicked out.

beats.content: @WithMockUser is an annotation from spring-security-test that creates a mock Authentication in the SecurityContext before your test runs. By default it creates a user with username 'user' and role USER. You specify @WithMockUser(roles='ADMIN') to simulate an admin.

To test authorization properly, you need two test cases per secured method. First, the success case: the correct role runs the method without throwing. Second, the rejection case: the wrong role triggers AccessDeniedException. An unauthenticated call throws AuthenticationCredentialsNotFoundException instead.

content: @WithMockUser — creates a mock user with specified username and roles
@WithUserDetails('alice') — loads the real user through your UserDetailsService
AccessDeniedException — what to expect when authenticated user lacks the required role
AuthenticationCredentialsNotFoundException — what to expect when no authentication exists at all

beats.content: non-obvious: spring-security-test is included transitively through spring-boot-starter-test — you don't need to add it separately. But the @SpringBootTest context is required for method security annotations to be active, since they work via AOP.

speakable_v2.cap: Always test both the authorized path and the rejection path. @WithMockUser for role simulation, assertThrows for AccessDeniedException — that's a complete security test.
followup_handoff: @WithUserDetails is more realistic than @WithMockUser — it loads the actual user from your database, which catches authorization bugs that mock users miss.
MockMvc security tests for controllers use springSecurity() in the setup to apply the full filter chain.
